preference_rationale: In-line results are less interesting; the payoff is in capturing sizable deviations from consensus, high or low. B is built for that. It winnows to the names where this information would actually be captured in the first place, and applies per-company inclusion screens and per-company shrunk coefficients rather than resting on a single pooled elasticity. It is also careful to decompose ARR into its two pieces and to speak plainly about what the data can track (seats) and what it cannot (pricing growth). The negative control A carries is not really relevant here: the point is out-of-sample performance per name, backtested and evaluated statistically.
critique_A: Leads with a validation that leaks. The headline is a random 20% company-quarter holdout, and the plan states in the same breath that random splits leak, then relegates rolling-origin to a gate. For a panel with company fixed effects and serially correlated ARR, a random company-quarter split trains on quarters that postdate the ones it predicts for the same company, so the headline number is not a clean out-of-sample result. The honest validation exists in the plan but is not what gets reported.
critique_B:
The gate is too strict in one specific way. Requiring beta in [0.5, 1.5] and separately testing beta = 1 constrains a magnitude that should not be constrained for this use. The right form is a positive, significant MAU correlation estimated independently for each company, with no regard to the magnitude of beta. A gate that kills a real per-name signal because a pooled elasticity falls outside a pre-set band has failed at the thing it was built to protect.

The thinness of the seat-disclosing gate sample is not an objection here. Because the output is per-name, an analysis that works on even one or two relevant companies is fine provided it is defensible on those names.
why_loser_was_defensible: A would have been the better plan if the question were whether MAU growth is in general indicative of ARR growth - that is a cross-sectional claim and a panel is the right instrument for it. But we are trading individual names, so per-company analysis is what the output has to support.
